section_summaries.epidemiology: Group A Streptococcus (GAS) infections have the highest burden in resource-limited settings, driven by poverty, overcrowding, and reduced access to medical care, with geography and climate also playing a role. Pharyngitis is the most common manifestation, peaking in school-aged children, with incidence 4-8 times higher in resource-limited settings. Impetigo is also common, especially in humid tropical locations. Invasive GAS infections, including cellulitis, erysipelas, necrotizing fasciitis, and streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (STSS), occur sporadically, with increasing incidence of cellulitis with age and significant mortality (10-20%). Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF) and Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD) are uncommon in industrialized settings but remain a major burden in Indigenous populations and resource-limited countries, accounting for significant global morbidity and mortality (over 639,000 deaths annually). Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN) is declining in industrialized settings but persists in tropical regions, often linked to pyoderma.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: The oropharynx and skin are the primary ecological niches for Group A Streptococcus (GAS) and major entry sites for infection. GAS adheres to mucosal or skin epithelium via surface proteins, notably M protein, which extends as hairlike filaments and, along with the hyaluronic acid capsule, helps GAS evade phagocytosis by blocking opsonization and complement fixation. Highly virulent strains can secrete superantigens, stimulating T lymphocytes and antigen-presenting cells, leading to overwhelming cytokine production and the shock seen in STSS. While antibodies to GAS proteins are important for protection, aberrant immune responses to benign GAS infections of the throat or skin can lead to immune-mediated sequelae like Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF), Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD), and Acute Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (APSGN). Genetic predispositions and cross-reactive antibodies are thought to play a role in ARF development, affecting endocardial, synovial, and neural tissues. APSGN involves activation of the alternative complement pathway.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: GAS infections present with a diverse spectrum, from benign self-limited throat and skin infections to lethal multi-organ failure. Pharyngitis often causes high fever, lymphadenopathy, and tonsillar exudates, resolving in 3-5 days, with potential suppurative complications like abscesses. Scarlet fever manifests as a diffuse blanching sandpaper-like rash, desquamation, and 'strawberry tongue', historically lethal. Impetigo involves superficial crusted skin lesions, potentially forming pustular or ulcerative lesions in tropical settings. Invasive infections include erysipelas (painful, demarcated dermal inflammation) and cellulitis (deeper, diffuse subcutaneous tissue infection), often with systemic toxicity. Necrotizing fasciitis is a rapidly progressing deep tissue infection leading to shock and multi-organ failure. STSS, typically associated with necrotizing fasciitis, involves hypotension and multi-organ dysfunction. Non-suppurative sequelae include ARF, characterized by fever, arthritis, carditis, erythema marginatum, chorea, and subcutaneous nodules, which can progress to RHD. APSGN presents with hematuria, edema, and hypertension 1-2 weeks after infection, usually benign in children but potentially severe in adults.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Diagnosis of GAS pharyngitis can be presumptive, based on culturing beta-hemolytic gram-positive cocci or using rapid antigen detection tests to differentiate from viral pharyngitis. Other beta-hemolytic streptococci (Groups C and G) must be differentiated. Staphylococcus aureus is a key differential for pyogenic and invasive GAS infections, especially skin, osteo-articular, and necrotizing pneumonia, with Table 40.2 providing distinguishing features. Clinical suspicion of necrotizing fasciitis or myonecrosis requires prompt surgical confirmation, as imaging is often non-definitive. The diagnosis of primary ARF relies on the 2015 revised Jones criteria, which include clinical and investigational findings, notably echocardiography for subclinical carditis, alongside risk stratification. APSGN diagnosis requires acute nephritis symptoms, evidence of recent GAS infection (culture or serology), and a compatible complement profile (depressed C3 and CH50).
section_summaries.treatment: Penicillin remains the universally sensitive and preferred treatment for GAS infections, including pharyngitis. For penicillin hypersensitivity, erythromycin and newer macrolides can be used, though macrolide resistance is common in some areas. Treatment for pharyngitis aims to alleviate symptoms, shorten duration, and prevent complications like ARF and peritonsillar abscess, especially critical in high-incidence ARF populations. Impetigo can be treated with oral, intramuscular, or topical antibiotics, with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole being an alternative to penicillin. For invasive infections (e.g., erysipelas, perianal cellulitis), penicillin is the treatment of choice, but empirical broad-spectrum antimicrobials are often initiated before microbiologic confirmation. Severe infections like necrotizing fasciitis are managed with IV meropenem or piperacillin/tazobactam plus clindamycin (which reduces toxin production) and crucial surgical debridement, with vancomycin added if MRSA is suspected and IVIG for STSS.
section_summaries.prevention: Primary prophylaxis for simple GAS pharyngitis contacts is rarely indicated, but for severe invasive GAS infections, experts recommend treating close contacts with regimens combining rifampin with penicillin, or using cephalosporins/azithromycin, due to increasing penicillin resistance for carriage eradication. Secondary prophylaxis with intramuscular benzathine penicillin G (BPG) administered four times weekly for 10 years (or longer for established valve disease) is central to preventing recurrences of ARF and progression of RHD. In APSGN outbreaks linked to pyoderma, community-based BPG treatment for infected individuals and contacts can reduce nephritogenic GAS transmission. Additionally, skin hygiene measures, including scabies control, are important for prevention in resource-limited settings. Vaccine development is ongoing, with multi-valent vaccines targeting common emm types in clinical trials and other candidate vaccines based on conserved antigens approaching clinical trial phases.

tables.title: Differential Diagnosis for Selected GAS Infections and GAS-Related Syndromes
rows: • Coryza, rhinorrhea, and hoarseness are prominent features of rhinovirus and coronavirus-associated pharyngitis, which is usually non-exudative.
• Adenovirus may be exudative and associated with conjunctivitis (i.e., “pharyngoconjunctival fever”).

• EBV-associated pharyngitis is often part of “infectious mononucleosis” and is associated with prominent lymphadenopathy and systemic features (e.g., myalgias and atypical lymphocytosis ± elevated transaminases).
• CMV and HIV may both cause a “mononucleosis-like” illness.
• Enterovirus “herpangina” is associated with discrete ulcerative lesions of the posterior pharynx.
• A. haemolyticus is more common in adolescence and associated with a pleomorphic rash affecting the extensor surfaces and spreading to the neck and trunk.
• N. gonorrhoeae throat infection is often asymptomatic, but should be considered in sexually active individuals.
• M. pneumoniae and C. pneumoniae produce pharyngitis accompanied by lower respiratory symptoms.

• Diphtheria is marked by extreme toxicity and the development of a thick pharyngeal exudate. Death is commonly caused by toxin-mediated cardiac suppression or direct invasion of local structures and asphyxiation. Remains a risk in settings where vaccination programs are lacking.
• Primary HSV gingivostomatitis results in ulcerative lesions of the lips, tongue, and buccal mucosa associated with fever, pain, and drooling.

• Acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis is caused by infection with mixed anaerobes and oral spirochetes, results in painful inflammation and sloughing of the gums. Associated with limited nutrition and dental hygiene.

• F. necrophorum is implicated in the development of Lemierre's syndrome in otherwise healthy individuals (oropharyngeal infection, sepsis, jugular vein thrombosis, septic emboli). Associated with poor response to standard therapy/deterioration.
• Cocksackie virus is associated with hand-foot-and-mouth disease

• Measles and rubella should be considered, especially if unvaccinated or history of recent contact. Measles is associated with prodromal conjunctivitis and coryzal symptoms and Koplik's spots. Rubella is associated with post-auricular lymphadenopathy.
• Roseola rash associated with defervescence and affects younger children (infants) more than scarlet fever.
• Parvovirus “fifth disease or erythema infectiosum” associated with distinctive “slapped cheek” rash of face and reticular rash of limbs appearing after fever resolution.

• KD and SD associated with multiple symptoms and prolonged fever (>5 days). KD is also associated with conjunctivitis, edema of the hands and feet, and stomatitis. SD is associated with transient or “evanescent” rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, uveitis, ± arthritis.
• S. aureus impetigo is more commonly (but not always) bullous and may co-infect with GAS in pyodermatous impetigo.
Group C and G beta-hemolytic streptococci

• Scabies may result in crusted lesions and burrows that are itchy and involve the interdigital spaces or diffusely involve the trunk. Infestation may predispose to pyoderma. Co-infection requires concurrent treatment with scabicidal agents.
• Tinea causes superficial, scaly, non-exudative lesions frequently with central sparing.
• Eczema is itchy, often in limb flexures.
• HSV presents with localized vesicles and sometimes pain, ± local lymph gland enlargement.
• S. aureus usually associated with clear portal of entry (e.g., wound).
• Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas, and anaerobes are more common in immunocompromised hosts (e.g., diabetic foot infections) neutropenic hosts.
• P. multocida, E. corrodens, and anaerobes after human or animal bites
• Aeromonas species may be rapidly progressive and associated with water exposure.
• E. rhusiopathiae and contact dermatitis are not associated with toxicity and may be suspected because of distribution (e.g., on hands) and exposure history (e.g., meat worker).
• Unlike other forms of necrotizing fasciitis, group A Streptococcus necrotizing fasciitis is rarely associated with gas formation.

• Polymicrobial infection may be associated with abdominal surgery or an occult colonic source, typically involving the perineum and abdominal wall (Fournier’s gangrene) and in patients with diabetes or peripheral vascular disease.
• S. aureus is typically associated with skin breakage. MRSA causes 10%–30% of S. aureus necrotizing fasciitis.
• Clostridial “gas gangrene”: usually secondary to traumatic interruption of vascular supply to affected limb, colonic or obstetric origin. More frequent in drug users.
• V. vulnificus associated with underlying illnesses and water exposure.
• Candida spp. and mucormycetes associated with immunosuppression/trauma.
• S. aureus is usually monoarticular. Associated with sepsis and moderate-to-severe toxicity if multifocal. Effusions are purulent and usually (but not always) culture-positive.

• PSRA associated with small joints and absence of other clinical features of acute rheumatic fever or a propensity to rheumatic heart disease. A diagnosis of PSRA should rarely be made in populations with a high incidence of acute rheumatic fever, and all cases should be given at least 12 months of penicillin prophylaxis before re-evaluation.
• N. gonorrhoeae may be multi-focal and migratory and must be considered if sexually active. Associated with cutaneous lesions in disseminated disease. Culture of joint fluid is frequently negative.
• JIA, previously juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, is usually symmetric, non-migratory, and has a more gradual onset. Other features (e.g., iritis and serositis) may be present.
• Transient synovitis more frequently occurs in younger children, affects the hips, is self-resolving, and less associated with raised inflammatory markers and fever.
• SLE associated with raised antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) autoantibodies.
• Reactive arthritis is associated with rash of palms and soles, conjunctivitis, and urethritis.
• Infective endocarditis is diagnosed based on the modified Duke criteria.

• Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis distinguished by complement profile (low C3, low CH50, normal C4) and raised streptococcal serology titers, although these may be coincidentally raised in non-post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Anti-streptolysin O titer (ASOT) may be normal if post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis secondary to impetigo.
• SLE, MPGN, and glomerulonephritis of chronic disease are also associated with low C3, which resolves slowly if untreated over 8 weeks or more.
• SLE is associated with depressed C4 and other manifestations (e.g., arthritis and/or iritis), positive ANA and dsDNA autoantibodies.
• MPGN presents with proteinuria, hematuria, and pyuria. Patients also have increased risk of chronic kidney disease (CKD).

• Glomerulonephritis of chronic disease is associated with endocarditis, chronic hepatitis B or C, syphilis, and malaria. Distinguished from post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis by other features (e.g., fever, positive blood cultures, hepatitis, etc.).

• Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis is associated with progression to end-stage renal failure. Occasionally secondary to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis but may be secondary to SLE (ANA positive) or Wegener's granulomatosis (anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody [ANCA] positive).
